details:
**Revealing the Qur'an to Muhammad**
Gabriel's most important role in Islam, where he is called Jibril (Jibra'il), and the most common giveaway. He served as the medium through which God revealed the Qur'an to Muhammad over roughly twenty-three years.

**"Read!" in the Cave of Hira**
Gabriel first appeared to Muhammad in the Cave of Hira on the mountain Jabal al-Nour near Mecca, embraced him, and commanded "Read!" (or "Recite!" / "Proclaim!") to the illiterate prophet. He then revealed the opening verses of Surah al-Alaq ("The Clot"), the first revelation, on the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr).

**Buraq and the Night Journey**
Gabriel brought Buraq, a winged, white heavenly steed described as smaller than a mule but larger than a donkey, for Muhammad to ride on the Isra and Mi'raj, the Night Journey from Mecca to Jerusalem and ascent through the heavens. Gabriel accompanied Muhammad but did not ride Buraq himself.

**The Annunciation to Mary**
In Christianity, Gabriel announced to the Virgin Mary that she would conceive and give birth to Jesus, an event called the Annunciation. In the Qur'an, he appears to Maryam as a "perfectly formed man" and breathes into her to bring about the conception.

**Striking Zechariah mute**
Gabriel announced to the elderly priest Zechariah that his wife Elizabeth would bear a son, John the Baptist (Yahya). When Zechariah asked "Whereby shall I know this?" in disbelief, Gabriel struck him mute until the child was named.

**Interpreting Daniel's visions**
In the Book of Daniel, Gabriel is one of only two angels named in the Hebrew Bible. He explains Daniel's vision of a ram (representing Media and Persia) destroyed by a he-goat (representing Greece under Alexander), and he delivers the prophecy of the Seventy Weeks of years.

**Hadith of Gabriel**
A famous hadith reported by Umar in which Gabriel, appearing as a man with jet-black hair and very white clothes, questions Muhammad about Islam, faith (iman), and ihsan, and about the signs of the Hour, such as a slave woman giving birth to her mistress. It defines the Five Pillars of Islam and is often regarded as one of the most important hadiths in Sunni Islam.

**Opening of Muhammad's chest**
While the young Muhammad was living with his foster mother Halima, Gabriel split open the boy's chest, removed his heart, and washed it in a golden vessel (with Zamzam water in some versions) before returning it. Some accounts say he filled it with wisdom and faith.

**Blowing the horn on Judgment Day**
In Christian popular tradition and African American spirituals, Gabriel blows a trumpet to announce the Second Coming and the Last Judgment. In Islam this role is usually given to the angel Israfil.

**Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah**
In Islamic and Jewish tradition, Gabriel was among the angels sent to rescue Lot and destroy Sodom and Gomorrah; one story says he lifted the cities on his wing. Jewish tradition also credits him with destroying the army of the Assyrian king Sennacherib.

**Well of Zamzam**
In Islamic tradition, when Hagar (Hajar) and her infant son Ishmael (Ismail) were dying of thirst in the desert, Gabriel struck the ground with his heel or wing to bring forth the Well of Zamzam in Mecca. Other versions credit the baby Ishmael with kicking the ground.

**Gabriel in the Book of Enoch**
In the apocryphal Book of Enoch, God sends Gabriel against the Nephilim, the giant offspring of the Watchers (fallen angels) and human women, provoking them to destroy one another in war.

**Gabriel at the Battle of Badr**
Islamic tradition holds that Gabriel led angels who fought alongside the Muslims at the Battle of Badr in 624, where they defeated the Quraysh of Mecca. He is also said to have aided Muhammad at the Battle of Uhud.

**Gabriel as Noah in Mormonism**
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints teaches that the angel Gabriel is the same being as the prophet Noah, who lived as a mortal before his angelic role.

**The Holy Spirit and "the Trustworthy"**
Muslims commonly interpret references to the "Holy Spirit" (Ruh al-Qudus) and the "Trustworthy Spirit" in the Qur'an as referring to Gabriel. He is also traditionally seen as the figure described in Surah an-Najm ("The Star").
